If it's async data, you may be reading before the fetch resolves; wait for it.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot destructure property '([^']+)' of '([^']+)' as it is (?:undefined|null)
patterns.title: Destructuring from null/undefined
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote `const {{ {1} }} = {2}` but `{2}` is `null` or `undefined`, so there's nothing to pull `{1}` out of.
fixes: Default the source: `const {{ {1} }} = {2} || {{}}`.
In a function param: `function f({{ {1} }} = {{}}) {{ ... }}`.
Check why `{2}` is empty — an unresolved promise or a missing return are the usual culprits.

patterns.title: Spreading/looping a non-iterable
patterns.diagnosis: You used `for...of`, array destructuring, or spread on `{1}`, but `{1}` isn't iterable. Plain objects and `undefined`/`null` are not iterable.
fixes: To loop a plain object's values use `Object.values({1})`; for keys use `Object.keys({1})`.
If `{1}` may be `undefined`, default it: `[...( {1} ?? [] )]`.
Iterating a NodeList/Map/Set works, but a bare object literal does not — convert it first.

patterns.title: Calling new on a non-constructor
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote `new {1}(...)` but `{1}` isn't a constructor — it may be a plain function, an object, or an import that doesn't expose what you think.
fixes: Check the import shape: a default export needs `import X from`, a named one needs `import {{ X }} from`.
Don't use `new` on arrow functions or plain factory functions — just call them.
Confirm `{1}` is actually a class/function with `console.log(typeof {1})`.

patterns.title: Unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: The parser hit `{1}` somewhere it can't appear. Usually a missing/extra comma, bracket, or parenthesis just before this point, or JSX/TS syntax in a plain `.js` file.
fixes: Look at the line just BEFORE the reported one — a missing `,` `)` or `}` is common.
If `{1}` is `<`, you're using JSX in a file the tool isn't treating as JSX/TSX.
Run the file through a linter/formatter (Prettier, ESLint) — it pinpoints the break.
Check for a stray trailing comma in a function call in old environments.

patterns.title: Truncated JSON / unbalanced brackets
patterns.diagnosis: The parser ran out of input before the structure closed. With `JSON.parse`, the JSON string is empty or cut off; in source code, a `{`, `(`, or `[` was never closed.
fixes: If it's `JSON.parse`, log the raw string first — an empty body or failed fetch gives `''`.
Guard parsing: `text ? JSON.parse(text) : null`.
In source, count your braces/parens — an editor's bracket-match highlight finds the unclosed one.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<', "(.*)" is not valid JSON
patterns.title: Got HTML where JSON was expected
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.json()` on a response whose body starts with `{1}` — that's HTML (often a 404/500 error page or your SPA's index.html), not JSON.
fixes: Check the request URL — a wrong path or proxy misconfig returns the HTML index page.
Inspect `res.status` and `res.headers.get('content-type')` before calling `.json()`.
Look at the response in the Network tab to see what the server actually sent.
patterns.example_fix:
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const data = await res.json();

patterns.title: Variable is not defined
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is used but was never declared in any reachable scope — a typo, a missing import, or a variable defined in a different scope/file.
fixes: Check the spelling and casing of `{1}`.
If `{1}` comes from a module, add the `import`/`require` for it.
If it's a browser global only in some environments (like `process` or `require`), it won't exist there.
Declare it with `let`/`const` before use.

patterns.title: Reassigning a const
patterns.diagnosis: You declared a binding with `const` and then assigned to it again. `const` forbids reassignment of the binding (though object contents can still mutate).
fixes: If the value needs to change, declare it with `let` instead of `const`.
If you only want to mutate object/array contents, do `obj.x = 1` or `arr.push(...)` — don't reassign the variable.
Check you didn't shadow a `const` you meant to update elsewhere.

patterns.title: Calling something that isn't a function
patterns.diagnosis: You put `()` after `{1}`, but at runtime `{1}` isn't a function — it's undefined, a different type, or a method that doesn't exist on this object/version.
fixes: Typo check: array `.forEach`/`.map`/`.includes`, string `.padStart` — confirm the method name and casing.
Log `typeof {1}` right before the call to see what it really is.
If `{1}` is an import, verify the export name and shape (default vs named).
A method like `.flat()`/`.at()` may be missing in an old runtime — polyfill or update.

patterns.title: Setting a property on null/undefined
patterns.diagnosis: You tried `something.{1} = ...` but `something` is `null` or `undefined`, so there's no object to set `{1}` on.
fixes: Initialize the container first: `obj = obj || {{}}` then `obj.{1} = ...`.
For nested paths, build each level: `a.b = a.b || {{}}; a.b.{1} = ...`.
If it's a DOM node, your selector probably matched nothing — check the element exists.

patterns.match: TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON
patterns.title: Circular reference in JSON.stringify
patterns.diagnosis: `JSON.stringify` hit an object that references itself (directly or via a cycle), so it can't produce finite JSON.
fixes: Pass a replacer that drops the cyclic keys, or use a library like `flatted`.
Common with DOM nodes, React fibers, or objects holding their own parent — stringify a plain subset instead.
Build a clean DTO with only the fields you need before stringifying.

patterns.title: fetch() failed before getting a response
patterns.diagnosis: The request never completed — it's a network-level failure, not an HTTP error. Common causes: CORS rejection, wrong/unreachable URL, offline, mixed content, or a blocked request.
fixes: Open the Network tab — a CORS block shows there even though JS only sees a generic failure.
Verify the URL and that the server is running and reachable.
An HTTPS page calling an HTTP URL (mixed content) gets blocked — use HTTPS for both.
An ad-blocker/extension or a CORS preflight failure can also cause this.

patterns.match: DOMException: Failed to execute 'querySelector(?:All)?' on 'Document': '([^']*)' is not a valid selector
patterns.title: Invalid CSS selector
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a valid CSS selector, so `querySelector` rejected it. Often an interpolated value with bad characters, a leading digit on an id, or stray quotes/spaces.
fixes: Ids/classes can't start with a digit unescaped — use `[id="{1}"]` for arbitrary values.
If you're building the selector from a string, escape it with `CSS.escape(value)`.
Double-check brackets and quotes are balanced inside the selector.

patterns.match: Uncaught DOMException: Failed to execute 'appendChild' on 'Node': parameter 1 is not of type 'Node'
patterns.title: appendChild given a non-Node
patterns.diagnosis: `appendChild` expects a DOM Node, but you passed something else — a string, `null`, an array, or a plain object.
fixes: To add text, use `el.append(str)` or set `el.textContent`, not `appendChild` with a string.
If the child came from `getElementById`/`querySelector`, it may be `null` — check it exists.
Create the node first: `const n = document.createElement('div')`, then append `n`.

patterns.match: Uncaught TypeError: ([\w.]+)\.addEventListener is not a function
patterns.title: addEventListener on a non-element
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't a DOM element/EventTarget, so it has no `addEventListener`. Most often the selector returned `null`, or `{1}` is a NodeList/array rather than a single element.
fixes: If you used `querySelectorAll` (or `getElementsByClassName`), loop: `[...nodes].forEach(n => n.addEventListener(...))`.
If the element is `null`, the script may run before the DOM is ready — move it to the bottom or wrap in `DOMContentLoaded`.
Verify the selector actually matches an element on the page.

patterns.match: Uncaught SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules
patterns.title: await outside an async function
patterns.diagnosis: You used `await` inside a regular (non-async) function, or in a script that isn't an ES module, where top-level `await` isn't allowed.
fixes: Mark the enclosing function `async`: `async function f() { await ... }`.
Inside callbacks (`.forEach`, `.map`), make the callback itself `async`.
For top-level await, run the file as an ES module (`.mjs` or `"type": "module"`), or wrap in an async IIFE.

patterns.title: Unhandled promise rejection
patterns.diagnosis: A promise rejected with `{1}` and nothing caught it. In modern Node this can crash the process.
fixes: Wrap awaited calls in `try/catch`, or add `.catch(...)` to the promise chain.
Make sure every `async` function called fire-and-forget has its own error handling.
Add a top-level guard: `process.on('unhandledRejection', err => ...)` for logging.

patterns.match: Error \[ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND\]: Cannot find module '([^']+)' imported from (.+)
patterns.title: ESM module not found
patterns.diagnosis: In ES-module mode, the import of `{1}` from `{2}` failed. ESM requires the file extension on relative imports and doesn't do CommonJS-style resolution.
fixes: Add the explicit extension: `import x from './util.js'`, not `'./util'`.
Confirm `{1}` exists at that path and the casing matches.
If it's a package, install it and check it ships an ESM/`exports` entry.

patterns.match: Error \[ERR_REQUIRE_ESM\]: require\(\) of ES Module (.+) (?:from (.+) )?not supported
patterns.title: require() of an ES Module
patterns.diagnosis: You used `require()` to load `{1}`, but that package is ESM-only. CommonJS `require` can't synchronously load an ES module.
fixes: Use dynamic import instead: `const mod = await import('the-package')`.
Convert your file to ESM (`"type": "module"` in package.json) and use `import`.
Check if the package ships an older CommonJS version you can pin to.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: The requested module '([^']+)' does not provide an export named '([^']+)'
patterns.title: Named import doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote `import {{ {2} }} from '{1}'`, but `{1}` has no export called `{2}`. Either the name is wrong, or it's a default export.
fixes: If `{2}` is the default export, use `import {2} from '{1}'` (no braces).
Check the exact exported name and casing in `{1}`.
For a CommonJS package consumed from ESM, try `import pkg from '{1}'` then `pkg.{2}`.

patterns.match: TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
patterns.title: reduce() on an empty array
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.reduce(fn)` on an empty array without an initial value, so there's no starting accumulator and nothing to return.
fixes: Always pass an initial value: `arr.reduce(fn, 0)` or `arr.reduce(fn, [])`.
Guard the array isn't unexpectedly empty before reducing.
Pick an initial value that matches your accumulator's type (number, array, object).
patterns.example_fix: const sum = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

patterns.title: toFixed digits out of range
patterns.diagnosis: `Number.prototype.toFixed` (or a similar method) got a digit count outside its allowed range (0–100).
fixes: Clamp the precision: `Math.min(Math.max(n, 0), 100)` before passing it.
Check the value isn't `NaN`, negative, or accidentally huge.
For plain rounding, `Math.round(x * 100) / 100` avoids the argument limits.

patterns.title: String grew too large
patterns.diagnosis: A string operation produced a string longer than the engine's max (~2^29 chars in V8). Usually an unbounded loop appending to a string, or a runaway `repeat`/`join`.
fixes: Look for a loop that concatenates without a stopping condition.
Build large output in an array and `join` once, or stream it instead of holding it all in memory.
Check arguments to `String.prototype.repeat` — a huge count blows the limit.

patterns.title: Invalid repeat count
patterns.diagnosis: `String.prototype.repeat` got a count that's negative or infinite (you passed `{1}`). The count must be a finite, non-negative integer.
fixes: Ensure the count is >= 0 and finite before calling `.repeat()`.
Guard against `NaN`/`Infinity` from a calculation feeding the count.
Floor the value if it might be fractional: `str.repeat(Math.max(0, Math.floor(n)))`.

patterns.title: Writing to a read-only property
patterns.diagnosis: In strict mode you assigned to `{1}`, but it's non-writable — a frozen object, a getter-only property, or a module export binding.
fixes: If the object is frozen (`Object.freeze`), clone it before changing: `{{ ...obj, key: val }}`.
You can't reassign an imported binding — change it in its source module instead.
A getter-only property needs a matching setter to accept assignment.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot add property ([^,]+), object is not extensible
patterns.title: Adding a key to a non-extensible object
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to add the new property `{1}` to an object sealed/frozen with `Object.freeze`, `Object.seal`, or `Object.preventExtensions`.
fixes: Spread into a new object to add fields: `const next = {{ ...obj, {1}: value }}`.
Don't mutate frozen state (common in Redux/immutable patterns) — produce a new object.
If you control the freeze, remove it or set all keys before freezing.

patterns.title: Object operation on null/undefined
patterns.diagnosis: An `Object.*` method (like `Object.keys`, `Object.entries`, `Object.assign` target) or a spread got `null`/`undefined` instead of an object.
fixes: Default the value: `Object.keys(obj ?? {})`.
Check the variable isn't an unresolved fetch result or a missing function return.
For `Object.assign`, the first argument (target) must be a real object.

patterns.title: BigInt/Symbol type mismatch
patterns.diagnosis: You mixed a BigInt or Symbol with an incompatible type — e.g. adding a BigInt to a regular number, or coercing a Symbol into a string implicitly.
fixes: Don't mix BigInt and Number in arithmetic — convert with `Number(big)` or `BigInt(num)` first (mind precision loss).
To stringify a Symbol, call `String(sym)` or `sym.toString()` explicitly.
Keep BigInt math entirely in BigInt: use `10n` literals throughout.

patterns.title: API called in an invalid state
patterns.diagnosis: A Web API method ('{1}') was invoked while the object was in a state that doesn't allow it — e.g. reading a response body twice, or using an IndexedDB/WebSocket before it's ready.
fixes: A fetch `Response` body can be consumed only once — `clone()` it if you need it twice.
Wait for the ready event (WebSocket `open`, IndexedDB `onsuccess`) before calling methods.
Check you're not reusing a one-shot object after it's already been read/closed.

patterns.title: .map on a non-array
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.map` on `{1}`, but `{1}` isn't an array. It's often `undefined` (data not loaded yet), a plain object, or an API response wrapped in another shape.
fixes: Default to an array: `({1} ?? []).map(...)` so it's safe before data arrives.
If `{1}` is a plain object, map its entries: `Object.entries({1}).map(...)`.
Inspect the API payload — the array might be nested, e.g. `{1}.items.map(...)`.
For a NodeList, convert first: `[...{1}].map(...)`.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot read propert(?:y|ies) of undefined \(reading '([^']+)'\) at ([\w.$]+)
patterns.title: TypeError — undefined property in {2}
patterns.diagnosis: Inside `{2}` you reached for `.{1}` on a value that was `undefined`. The object up the chain never got set, or a function returned nothing.
fixes: Log the object just before the `.{1}` access to see why it's undefined.
Guard with optional chaining: `obj?.{1}`.
Provide a default: `const x = obj ?? {{}}` before reading `.{1}`.

patterns.title: TypeError — `{1}` can't be spread/destructured
patterns.diagnosis: You used `{1}` in a `for...of`, array destructuring, or spread (`...`), but `{1}` isn't iterable. Plain objects, `null`, `undefined`, and numbers aren't iterable.
fixes: If `{1}` is an object, iterate keys with `Object.entries({1})` or `Object.keys({1})`.
If `{1}` might be null/undefined, default it: `for (const x of {1} ?? []) {{}}`.
If `{1}` is array-like (NodeList, arguments), convert first: `Array.from({1})`.
patterns.example_fix: for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) console.log(k, v);

patterns.match: TypeError: ([\w.$]+)(?:\.[\w$]+)?\(\.\.\.\) is not a function|([\w.$]+)\.map is not a function
patterns.title: TypeError — `.map`/method on a non-array
patterns.diagnosis: You called an array method (like `.map`, `.filter`, `.forEach`) on something that isn't an array. Often the value is an object, `undefined`, or a fetch response you forgot to `.json()`.
fixes: Confirm the value is an array: `console.log(Array.isArray(x), x)`.
If it's an API response, did you `await res.json()` first?
If it's an object, use `Object.values(x).map(...)`.
Default to an empty array: `(x ?? []).map(...)`.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: Unexpected token '?<'|SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input
patterns.title: SyntaxError — unexpected end of input
patterns.diagnosis: The parser reached the end of the file while still expecting more — usually an unclosed `{`, `(`, `[`, or a string/template literal that never closed.
fixes: Count your brackets — most editors highlight the matching pair when you click one.
Look for an unterminated string or backtick template literal.
Run the file through a linter (`eslint`) or Prettier to pinpoint the location.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: (?:Unexpected token .{0,3} in JSON at position (\d+)|.{0,60} is not valid JSON)
patterns.title: SyntaxError — bad JSON near position {1}
patterns.diagnosis: `JSON.parse` choked at character {1}. JSON is strict: trailing commas, single quotes, unquoted keys, and comments are all illegal.
fixes: Remove trailing commas — no comma after the last array element or object property.
Use double quotes for all keys and string values, never single quotes.
Paste the string into a JSON validator to see the exact bad character at {1}.
If this is a fetch response, log the raw text — it may be HTML (an error page), not JSON.

patterns.match: SyntaxError: "undefined" is not valid JSON|SyntaxError: Unexpected token u in JSON at position 0
patterns.title: SyntaxError — parsing `undefined` as JSON
patterns.diagnosis: `JSON.parse(undefined)` was called. The value handed in was the literal `undefined` (or the string "undefined"), often from a missing localStorage key or an empty response body.
fixes: Guard before parsing: `const data = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;`.
`localStorage.getItem(key)` returns `null` for missing keys — check for it.
Log the raw value before parsing to confirm what you actually received.
patterns.example_fix:
const saved = localStorage.getItem('cart');
const cart = saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : [];

patterns.match: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.*JSON\.stringify|TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON
patterns.title: Circular reference in JSON.stringify
patterns.diagnosis: `JSON.stringify` hit an object that references itself (directly or through a chain). JSON can't represent cycles.
fixes: Break the cycle before stringifying, or omit the back-reference property.
Use a replacer that tracks seen objects and drops repeats.
For debugging, `util.inspect(obj, {{ depth: null }})` (Node) handles cycles.

patterns.title: TypeError — `{1}` isn't a constructor
patterns.diagnosis: You used `new {1}(...)` but `{1}` isn't a class or constructor function. Common with a bad import (got the module object instead of the class) or `new` on a regular function/arrow.
fixes: Check the import shape: `const {{ {1} }} = require('...')` vs `const {1} = require('...')`.
Arrow functions can't be used with `new` — use a `class` or `function`.
Log `typeof {1}` — it should be `'function'` for `new` to work.

patterns.match: TypeError: ([\w.$]+) is not a function or its return value is not iterable
patterns.title: TypeError — iterator protocol on `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: Destructuring or spread tried to use `{1}` as an iterable, but its `[Symbol.iterator]` is missing or not a function. Often `{1}` is a plain object being array-destructured.
fixes: Use object destructuring `{{ }}` instead of array destructuring `[ ]` for plain objects.
Confirm `{1}` is actually an array or Map/Set, not an object literal.
If you wrote a custom iterator, ensure `[Symbol.iterator]` returns an object with a `next()` method.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property '([^']+)' of object
patterns.title: TypeError — `{1}` is read-only
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to write to `{1}`, but it's non-writable — the object is frozen (`Object.freeze`), the prop was defined with `writable: false`, or it's a getter-only property.
fixes: If the object is frozen, clone it first: `const copy = {{ ...obj, {1}: newVal }}`.
Check for `Object.freeze` / `Object.defineProperty` on this object.
In React/Redux, never mutate state directly — return a new object.

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot add property ([\w$]+), object is not extensible
patterns.title: TypeError — can't add `{1}` to a sealed object
patterns.diagnosis: You added a new property `{1}` to an object that was sealed or frozen (`Object.seal` / `Object.freeze` / `Object.preventExtensions`). New keys aren't allowed.
fixes: Spread into a new object instead: `const next = {{ ...obj, {1}: value }}`.
Find where the object got frozen/sealed and decide if it should be.
If this is framework state, use the framework's update API rather than mutating.

patterns.title: TypeError — awaiting a non-promise method `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: You `await`ed or called `{1}(...)` expecting a promise/function, but it isn't one here. Often a typo in the method name, or the object isn't the type you think (e.g., not an Axios/fetch instance).
fixes: Check the method name spelling and that the library exposes it.
Log the object to confirm its type before calling `{1}`.
If it's a dynamic import, `await import('...')` returns the module namespace.

patterns.match: DOMException: Failed to execute 'querySelector' on 'Document': '([^']+)' is not a valid selector
patterns.title: Invalid CSS selector — `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: `querySelector('{1}')` was handed a malformed CSS selector. Common causes: a selector starting with a digit, an unescaped special char, or passing a raw ID/variable instead of a selector string.
fixes: IDs/classes need a prefix: `#myId` or `.myClass`, not just `myId`.
If the ID starts with a digit, use `getElementById` or escape it with `CSS.escape`.
Building a selector from a variable? Use `document.getElementById(id)` instead.

patterns.match: Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null \(reading '(addEventListener|value|textContent|innerHTML|style|classList)'\)
patterns.title: TypeError — element not found before `.{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: `getElementById`/`querySelector` returned `null`, then you accessed `.{1}` on it. The element doesn't exist yet (script ran before the DOM loaded) or the selector is wrong.
fixes: Move the `<script>` to the end of `<body>`, or add `defer` to the tag.
Wrap in `document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', ...)`.
Double-check the id/selector matches the HTML exactly (case-sensitive).
Guard it: `el && el.{1}`.

patterns.match: TypeError: Failed to fetch dynamically imported module: (.+)
patterns.title: Dynamic import failed — {1}
patterns.diagnosis: A `import('...')` at runtime couldn't load `{1}`. The path 404'd, the chunk was stale after a deploy, or the dev server isn't serving that file.
fixes: Verify the path/URL of `{1}` actually resolves in the network tab.
After a redeploy, old chunk hashes can vanish — prompt the user to hard-refresh.
Add a `.catch()` on the dynamic import to fall back gracefully.
In Vite, restart the dev server if the module was just added.

patterns.match: TypeError: NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource
patterns.title: fetch failed — network/CORS
patterns.diagnosis: Firefox's wording for a fetch that never completed. The server was unreachable, the URL was wrong, the request was blocked by CORS, or the connection dropped.
fixes: Open the URL directly in the browser to confirm it responds.
Check the Network tab — a CORS block shows there even when JS just sees a failure.
Verify the protocol/host/port; localhost vs 127.0.0.1 can differ.
Add error handling: `fetch(url).catch(err => ...)`.

patterns.match: Access to fetch at '([^']+)' from origin '([^']+)' has been blocked by CORS policy
patterns.title: CORS — {2} can't fetch {1}
patterns.diagnosis: The browser blocked a request from origin `{2}` to `{1}` because the server didn't return permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers. CORS is enforced by the browser, not your code.
fixes: Fix it on the server: send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: {2}` (or `*`).
For dev, proxy the request through your own dev server (Vite/CRA proxy).
Preflighted requests (custom headers, non-simple methods) need the server to handle `OPTIONS`.
You cannot fix CORS purely from the browser — it's a server-side header.

patterns.title: TypeError — `{1}` isn't a Promise
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.then()` on `{1}`, but it's not a thenable. Likely you forgot to call the async function (passed the function instead of its result), or the function returns a plain value.
fixes: Make sure you invoked it: `getData().then(...)`, not `getData.then(...)`.
If `{1}` returns a value synchronously, just use it directly — no `.then`.
Wrap a sync value in a promise if you really need chaining: `Promise.resolve({1})`.

patterns.title: ECONNREFUSED — nothing listening on {1}:{2}
patterns.diagnosis: A TCP connection to `{1}:{2}` was refused — no server is listening there, it crashed, or it's bound to a different host/port.
fixes: Confirm the target service is running and listening on port {2}.
Check the host — a server on `localhost` won't accept `{1}` if they differ.
Verify firewall/Docker port mapping exposes {2}.
Add a retry/backoff if the dependency starts slowly.

patterns.title: ENOTFOUND — can't resolve host `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: DNS lookup for `{1}` failed — the hostname doesn't resolve. Usually a typo in the URL, a missing protocol, or no network/DNS.
fixes: Check the hostname `{1}` for typos and that it includes no stray path/protocol.
Test resolution: `ping {1}` or `nslookup {1}`.
If it's an internal service, confirm you're on the right network/VPN.
Ensure the URL has a scheme: `https://{1}/...`.

patterns.title: Socket closed mid-transfer (EPIPE/ECONNRESET)
patterns.diagnosis: The other end of the connection went away while data was still flowing. The client closed the tab, a proxy timed out, or the upstream server reset the socket.
fixes: Handle the error on the stream/socket so it doesn't crash the process: `stream.on('error', ...)`.
For HTTP clients, add retries with backoff for transient resets.
Check for timeouts on a proxy or load balancer in front of your server.
These are often harmless on client disconnect — log and move on.

patterns.match: Error: connect ETIMEDOUT|(?:request|fetch) timed out after (\d+)ms
patterns.title: Connection timed out
patterns.diagnosis: The request didn't get a response in time. The remote host is unreachable, overloaded, or a firewall is silently dropping packets.
fixes: Verify the host/port are reachable and the service is healthy.
Raise the timeout if the operation is legitimately slow.
Add a retry with exponential backoff for flaky networks.
Check for a firewall dropping (not refusing) the connection.

patterns.match: FATAL ERROR: .*JavaScript heap out of memory
patterns.title: Out of memory — heap exhausted
patterns.diagnosis: The Node process used more memory than the V8 heap allows. Common causes: an unbounded array/cache, a leak retaining objects, or processing a huge file all at once.
fixes: Find what grows without bound — caches, arrays, event listeners.
Stream large files instead of reading them fully into memory.
Raise the limit as a stopgap: `node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js`.
Profile with `--inspect` + Chrome DevTools heap snapshots to find the leak.

patterns.title: Node warning — {1}
patterns.diagnosis: Node emitted a runtime warning: "{1}". It's not fatal, but it flags a deprecated API or a likely leak (e.g., too many listeners on one emitter).
fixes: For deprecation warnings, switch to the replacement API named in the message.
Run with `node --trace-warnings app.js` to get a stack trace to the source.
For MaxListeners: remove listeners when done, or `emitter.setMaxListeners(n)` if intentional.

patterns.match: error TS\d+|Type '([^']+)' is not assignable to type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: Type mismatch — `{1}` not assignable to `{2}`
patterns.diagnosis: TypeScript refused a value of type `{1}` where `{2}` was expected. The shapes don't line up, or one is wider/narrower than the other.
fixes: Narrow `{1}` to match `{2}` (e.g., handle `undefined`/`null` cases).
If you're sure, assert: `value as {2}` — but prefer fixing the real type.
Check for `strictNullChecks` flagging a possibly-undefined value.
Update the function signature if `{1}` is genuinely valid input.

patterns.title: Validation failed — `{1}`
patterns.diagnosis: A schema validator (Mongoose, Joi, Zod, Yup) rejected the data because `{1}` was missing or didn't match its rules.
fixes: Ensure `{1}` is present and the right type before saving/submitting.
Read the full message — it usually names the exact rule that failed.
Validate on the client too so users get feedback before the request.
If `{1}` should be optional, loosen the schema for that field.

patterns.match: MongoServerError: E11000 duplicate key error.*index: ([\w.$]+) dup key: \{ ([^:]+):
patterns.title: Mongo duplicate key on `{2}` (index {1})
patterns.diagnosis: An insert/update violated a unique index `{1}` — a document with the same `{2}` already exists. Mongo enforces uniqueness at the database level.
fixes: Check for an existing document with that `{2}` before inserting.
Use `updateOne(..., {{ upsert: true }})` if you meant to insert-or-update.
Catch code `11000` and surface a friendly "already exists" message.
If duplicates should be allowed, drop the unique index on `{2}`.

patterns.title: JWT expired
patterns.diagnosis: The JSON Web Token's `exp` claim is in the past, so verification rejected it. The user's session/token has timed out.
fixes: Refresh the token via your refresh-token flow, then retry.
On the client, treat this as "log in again" rather than a hard error.
Check server/client clock skew if tokens expire sooner than expected.
Don't blindly extend `expiresIn` — short-lived access tokens are the point.

patterns.match: Error \[ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT\]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client
patterns.title: Headers already sent (Express)
patterns.diagnosis: You called `res.send`/`res.json`/`res.end`/`res.redirect` more than once for the same request, or kept running code after responding. Each request can send headers only once.
fixes: Add `return` before `res.send(...)` so the handler stops there.
Check for a missing `else` — both branches may be responding.
In async middleware, make sure you don't call `next()` after sending a response.
Trace every path that touches `res` for this route.
patterns.example_fix:
if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'not found' });
res.json(user);

patterns.title: spawn {1} ENOENT — command not found
patterns.diagnosis: `child_process.spawn`/`exec` couldn't find the executable `{1}`. It's not installed, not on `PATH`, or on Windows you need the `.cmd` shim.
fixes: Confirm `{1}` is installed and on `PATH` (`which {1}`).
On Windows, npm-installed CLIs need `{1}.cmd` or `{{ shell: true }}`.
Pass the full absolute path to the binary instead of bare `{1}`.
Check the cwd you spawned in — relative paths resolve from there.

patterns.match: Warning: Can't perform a React state update on a component that hasn't mounted yet
patterns.title: React — setState before mount
patterns.diagnosis: A state setter fired before the component finished mounting, usually from a synchronous call in the render body or a constructor.
fixes: Move side effects into `useEffect` (or `componentDidMount`), not render.
Don't call setters directly during render — guard them in event handlers/effects.
If an async callback resolves before mount, check a mounted flag first.

patterns.match: Warning: A component is changing an? (?:un)?controlled input (?:of type \w+ )?to be (?:un)?controlled
patterns.title: React — controlled/uncontrolled input flip
patterns.diagnosis: An input's `value` went from `undefined`/`null` to a defined value (or vice versa). React can't tell if the input is controlled or not, so it warns.
fixes: Initialize state to `''` (empty string), never `undefined`.
Always pass a defined `value`: `value={state ?? ''}`.
Pick one mode: either always pass `value`+`onChange`, or use `defaultValue` and don't pass `value`.
patterns.example_fix:
const [name, setName] = useState('');
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />

patterns.match: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined \(reading 'map'\)
patterns.title: TypeError — `.map` on undefined (often React data)
patterns.diagnosis: You called `.map` on a value that's still `undefined` — classic with data that hasn't loaded yet (async fetch) or a prop that wasn't passed.
fixes: Default it: `(items ?? []).map(...)`.
Render a loading state until the data arrives: `if (!items) return <Spinner/>;`.
Initialize state to `[]` instead of `undefined`.
Give the prop a default value in the component signature.

patterns.title: TS2304 — can't find name
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler has no declaration in scope for `{1}`. It's misspelled, not imported, or its type definitions aren't installed.
fixes: Check the spelling and casing of `{1}`.
Import it: `import { {1} } from '...';`.
If `{1}` is a global from a runtime (e.g. `process`, `Buffer`), install the types: `npm i -D @types/node` and add that lib to tsconfig.
If it's a browser/DOM global, add `"dom"` to `compilerOptions.lib`.

patterns.match: error TS2552: Cannot find name '([^']+)'\. Did you mean '([^']+)'\?
patterns.title: TS2552 — did you mean a different name?
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` isn't declared in scope. The compiler thinks you meant `{2}`, which is in scope and spelled similarly.
fixes: Replace `{1}` with `{2}` if that's what you intended.
Otherwise import or declare `{1}` before using it.
Watch for casing — TypeScript identifiers are case-sensitive.

patterns.title: TS2300 — duplicate identifier
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is declared more than once in the same scope. This often comes from two `import`s of the same name, redeclaring a variable, or merging conflicting type declarations.
fixes: Remove or rename one of the declarations of `{1}`.
If two imports collide, alias one: `import { {1} as {1}Alt } from '...';`.
Check for a `.d.ts` that re-declares the same global as your code.

patterns.match: error TS2451: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2451 — can't redeclare block-scoped variable
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is declared twice with `let`/`const` in the same block. Unlike `var`, block-scoped bindings can't be redeclared.
fixes: Delete the second `let`/`const {1}` and just assign: `{1} = ...`.
Rename one of the two `{1}` bindings.
If this is a global script colliding with another file, wrap it in a module (add an `export {}` so the file becomes a module with its own scope).

patterns.match: error TS2454: Variable '([^']+)' is used before being assigned
patterns.title: TS2454 — used before assigned
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is declared but the compiler can't prove it was assigned a value on every path before this use.
fixes: Give `{1}` an initial value at declaration: `let {1} = ...`.
Assign `{1}` in every branch (each `if`/`else`/`case`) before reading it.
If you're sure it's set (e.g. by a callback), use a definite assignment assertion: `let {1}!: Type;`.

patterns.match: error TS2564: Property '([^']+)' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor
patterns.title: TS2564 — class property not initialized
patterns.diagnosis: With `strictPropertyInitialization`, the class field `{1}` must get a value at its declaration or inside the constructor, but the compiler can't see one.
fixes: Initialize at declaration: `{1} = defaultValue;`.
Assign `this.{1} = ...` in the constructor on every path.
If a framework/DI assigns it later, use a definite assignment assertion: `{1}!: Type;`.
Or make it optional: `{1}?: Type;`.

patterns.match: error TS7006: Parameter '([^']+)' implicitly has an 'any' type
patterns.title: TS7006 — parameter implicitly any
patterns.diagnosis: Under `noImplicitAny`, the parameter `{1}` has no annotation and the compiler can't infer its type, so it falls back to `any` — which strict mode forbids.
fixes: Annotate it: `({1}: string) => ...`.
If it's a callback, let the surrounding type infer it (e.g. give the array a type so `.map(x => ...)` infers `x`).
As a last resort: `({1}: any)` — but prefer a real type.
If this is intentional and widespread, relax `noImplicitAny` in tsconfig (not recommended).

patterns.match: error TS7053: Element implicitly has an 'any' type because expression of type '([^']+)' can't be used to index type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS7053 — implicit any from indexing
patterns.diagnosis: You're indexing `{2}` with a `{1}` key, but `{2}` has no matching index signature, so the result would be `any`.
fixes: Add an index signature to the type: `{ [key: string]: Value }`.
Use `keyof typeof obj` for the key so TS knows it's valid: `obj[k as keyof typeof obj]`.
Use a `Record<string, Value>` or a `Map` instead of a plain object.
Narrow the key to a known literal union before indexing.
patterns.example_fix: const v = obj[key as keyof typeof obj];

patterns.match: error TS2722: Cannot invoke an object which is possibly 'undefined'
patterns.title: TS2722 — calling a possibly-undefined function
patterns.diagnosis: The value you're calling might be `undefined` at runtime, so invoking it could throw.
fixes: Guard it: `if (fn) fn();`.
Use optional chaining for the call: `fn?.();`.
Provide a default: `(fn ?? (() => {}))();`.
If the type wrongly includes `undefined`, fix the declaration to make it required.

patterns.title: TS18048 — possibly undefined
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can be `undefined` at this point, so accessing a property or calling it could fail at runtime.
fixes: Guard before use: `if ({1}) { ... }`.
Use optional chaining: `{1}?.prop`.
Supply a fallback: `{1} ?? defaultValue`.
If you're certain it's defined, assert: `{1}!` (use sparingly).

patterns.title: TS18047 — possibly null
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` can be `null` here (commonly from `document.querySelector`, `getElementById`, or a nullable API result), so dereferencing it may throw.
fixes: Null-check first: `if ({1}) { ... }`.
Use optional chaining: `{1}?.method()`.
Use `??` for a fallback value.
If the DOM element definitely exists, assert: `{1}!` after confirming.

patterns.match: error TS2769: No overload matches this call
patterns.title: TS2769 — no matching overload
patterns.diagnosis: The function you're calling has multiple overload signatures and the arguments you passed don't fit any of them. The error text below usually lists each overload and why it failed.
fixes: Read the per-overload reasons under the error — fix the first argument the compiler complains about.
Check argument count and order against the overload signatures.
Make sure each argument's type matches (number vs string, object shape, etc.).
If you're passing a union, narrow it first so it matches one overload.

patterns.match: error TS2349: This expression is not callable
patterns.title: TS2349 — not callable
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote `()` after something whose type has no call signature — it isn't a function (often a value, a union including a non-function, or a namespace/type used as a value).
fixes: Remove the `()` if you meant the value, not a call.
If it's a union, narrow to the function member first.
Check you're not shadowing the function name with a variable.
If a property holds the function, call that property: `obj.fn()`.

patterns.match: error TS2554: Expected (\d+) arguments, but got (\d+)
patterns.title: TS2554 — wrong argument count
patterns.diagnosis: The function expects {1} argument(s) but you passed {2}.
fixes: Pass exactly {1} argument(s), or fix the call site.
If trailing args are optional, mark them in the signature: `(a: number, b?: string)`.
Use a default parameter so callers may omit it: `(b = 0)`.
For variadic functions, declare a rest parameter: `(...args: number[])`.

patterns.match: error TS2559: Type '([^']+)' has no properties in common with type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2559 — no overlapping properties
patterns.diagnosis: You assigned a `{1}` where a `{2}` is expected, but they share no properties — TypeScript treats this as almost certainly a mistake (e.g. passing an options object with all-wrong keys).
fixes: Check the property names against `{2}` — they're probably misspelled.
Make sure you're passing the right object to the right parameter.
If `{2}` is meant to allow extra/empty shapes, widen its type or mark fields optional.

patterns.match: error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and '([^']+)' does not exist in type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2353 — unknown property in object literal
patterns.diagnosis: Excess property check: the literal you're assigning to a `{2}` includes `{1}`, which isn't part of `{2}`. Literals get checked more strictly than variables.
fixes: Remove `{1}` or fix its spelling to a real property of `{2}`.
If `{1}` is legitimately extra, add it to the `{2}` type.
Assign through a variable first to skip excess-property checks (only if intentional).
Add an index signature to `{2}` if arbitrary extra keys are allowed.

patterns.match: error TS2367: This comparison appears to be unintentional because the types '([^']+)' and '([^']+)' have no overlap
patterns.title: TS2367 — comparison with no overlap
patterns.diagnosis: You're comparing a `{1}` with a `{2}` using `===`/`!==`. Their types can never be equal, so the comparison is always false (or always true for `!==`).
fixes: Check you're comparing the right variables — one is probably the wrong type.
If comparing an enum/literal union, make sure the literal you wrote is a member.
Convert one side first if you truly need a cross-type compare (e.g. `String(x) === y`).

patterns.match: error TS2741: Property '([^']+)' is missing in type '([^']+)' but required in type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2741 — missing required property
patterns.diagnosis: The value of type `{2}` you're assigning lacks `{1}`, which `{3}` requires.
fixes: Add `{1}` to the object you're constructing.
If `{1}` should be optional, mark it `{1}?:` in the `{3}` type.
If `{1}` has a sensible default, set it before assignment.
Double-check you didn't misspell `{1}`.

patterns.match: error TS2740: Type '([^']+)' is missing the following properties from type '([^']+)': (.+)
patterns.title: TS2740 — missing several properties
patterns.diagnosis: A `{1}` is being used as a `{2}`, but it's missing these properties: {3}.
fixes: Add the missing properties ({3}) to your object.
If you only have a partial value, type it as `Partial<{2}>`.
Make the missing fields optional in `{2}` if they're genuinely not always present.

patterns.match: error TS2416: Property '([^']+)' in type '([^']+)' is not assignable to the same property in base type '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2416 — override incompatible with base
patterns.diagnosis: Your subclass `{2}` declares `{1}` with a type that isn't compatible with `{1}` in the base type `{3}`.
fixes: Match the base signature for `{1}` (same parameter and return types).
Method parameters must be at least as general as the base (contravariant); return types at least as specific.
If you intended a different shape, the inheritance relationship is wrong — reconsider extending `{3}`.

patterns.match: error TS4114: This member must have an 'override' modifier because it overrides a member in the base class '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS4114 — missing override modifier
patterns.diagnosis: `noImplicitOverride` is on: a method here overrides one in base class `{1}`, so it must be marked `override`.
fixes: Add the `override` keyword: `override method() { ... }`.
If you did NOT mean to override, rename the method.
Make sure the base really has this member — typos can hide a true override.

patterns.match: error TS2515: Non-abstract class '([^']+)' does not implement inherited abstract member '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2515 — abstract member not implemented
patterns.diagnosis: Class `{1}` extends an abstract class but doesn't implement the abstract member `{2}`.
fixes: Implement `{2}` in `{1}`.
If `{1}` is also meant to be abstract, mark it `abstract class {1}`.
Check the method/property name and signature match the abstract declaration exactly.

patterns.match: error TS2420: Class '([^']+)' incorrectly implements interface '([^']+)'
patterns.title: TS2420 — class doesn't satisfy interface
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` claims to implement `{2}` but doesn't match its shape — a member is missing or has the wrong type (the lines below pinpoint which).
fixes: Add or fix the member named in the follow-up error.
Match each method's parameter and return types to `{2}`.
Make sure property modifiers (readonly, optional) line up with `{2}`.

patterns.title: TS1005 — token expected
patterns.diagnosis: A syntax error: the parser expected `{1}` at this position. Usually a missing comma, semicolon, brace, or a stray token.
fixes: Add the missing `{1}` where indicated.
Check the line just above — an unclosed `(`, `{`, or `[` often reports the error one line later.
Look for a misplaced keyword or a comma where a semicolon belongs.

patterns.title: TS1109 — expression expected
patterns.diagnosis: The parser hit a spot that needs a value/expression but found something else — often a dangling operator, an extra comma, or a reserved word used as a value.
fixes: Remove the trailing operator or comma before this point.
Make sure both sides of `=`, `?`, `:`, `&&`, etc. have real expressions.
Check for an unfinished arrow function or a `return` with nothing after it on the wrong line.

patterns.match: error TS1128: Declaration or statement expected
patterns.title: TS1128 — declaration or statement expected
patterns.diagnosis: The parser found a token where a new statement should begin — commonly an extra `}`, a stray `,`, or leftover JSX/code from a bad merge.
fixes: Look for an extra closing brace `}` or bracket above this line.
Remove any stray punctuation between statements.
Check for an unterminated block or object literal earlier in the file.

patterns.title: TS1110 — type expected
patterns.diagnosis: In a type position the parser expected a type but found something invalid — e.g. a dangling `|`/`&` in a union/intersection, or `:` with nothing after it.
fixes: Complete the annotation: `: SomeType`.
Remove a trailing `|` or `&` in a union/intersection type.
Don't use a value where a type is needed — use `typeof value` to get its type.

patterns.match: error TS1192: Module '"([^"]+)"' has no default export
patterns.title: TS1192 — module has no default export
patterns.diagnosis: You used a default import (`import X from '{1}'`) but module `{1}` only has named exports.
fixes: Use a named import: `import { Thing } from '{1}'`.
Use a namespace import: `import * as X from '{1}'`.
If it's a CommonJS module, enable `esModuleInterop` in tsconfig.
Add a real default export to `{1}` if you own it.

patterns.match: error TS1259: Module '"([^"]+)"' can only be default-imported using the 'esModuleInterop' flag
patterns.title: TS1259 — needs esModuleInterop
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is a CommonJS module being default-imported. TypeScript needs `esModuleInterop` to synthesize that default.
fixes: Set `"esModuleInterop": true` (and usually `"allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true`) in tsconfig.
Or import as namespace: `import * as x from '{1}'`.
Or use `import x = require('{1}')` with `"module": "commonjs"`.

patterns.match: error TS2614: Module '"([^"]+)"' has no exported member '([^']+)'\. Did you mean to use 'import ([^ ]+) from
patterns.title: TS2614 — named import should be default
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` doesn't export a named `{2}`; it's a default export. You used `{ {2} }` braces by mistake.
fixes: Drop the braces: `import {2} from '{1}'`.
Verify whether `{1}` uses default or named exports.
With CommonJS interop, a default import maps to `module.exports`.

patterns.match: error TS6133: '([^']+)' is declared but its value is never read
patterns.title: TS6133 — unused declaration
patterns.diagnosis: `noUnusedLocals`/`noUnusedParameters` is on and `{1}` is declared but never used.
fixes: Remove `{1}` if it's genuinely dead.
Use it where intended.
For an intentionally-unused parameter, prefix with `_`: `_{1}` (or set `"argsIgnorePattern"`).
Drop an unused import of `{1}`.

patterns.match: error TS2588: Cannot assign to '([^']+)' because it is a constant
patterns.title: TS2588 — assigning to a const
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` was declared with `const`, so it can't be reassigned.
fixes: Declare it with `let` if it needs to change.
Mutate the object/array contents instead of reassigning the binding.
If it's truly constant, the assignment is a logic bug — remove it.

patterns.match: error TS2540: Cannot assign to '([^']+)' because it is a read-only property
patterns.title: TS2540 — assigning to readonly property
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is marked `readonly` (or comes from a `readonly`/`as const` type), so it can't be reassigned after initialization.
fixes: Set `{1}` only in the constructor or at declaration.
If it must change, remove the `readonly` modifier.
Build a new object with the changed value instead of mutating: `{ ...obj, {1}: next }`.
If the type is `as const`, drop the assertion to make it mutable.

patterns.match: error TS2538: Type '([^']+)' cannot be used as an index type
patterns.title: TS2538 — invalid index type
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to index an object with a `{1}`, but object keys must be `string`, `number`, or `symbol`.
fixes: Narrow the key to a string/number first.
If `{1}` is a union, narrow it (e.g. `typeof key === 'string'`).
Use `String(key)` if a string key is appropriate.
Use a `Map` if you need non-primitive keys.

patterns.match: error TS2488: Type '([^']+)' must have a '\[Symbol\.iterator\]\(\)' method that returns an iterator
patterns.title: TS2488 — not iterable
patterns.diagnosis: You used a `{1}` in a spread/`for...of`/destructuring context, but it isn't iterable.
fixes: If it's array-like (e.g. NodeList, arguments), convert: `Array.from(value)`.
Make sure the value really is an array/iterable and not a plain object.
For objects, iterate `Object.entries(obj)` instead of `for...of obj`.
If targeting older JS, enable `"downlevelIteration": true` in tsconfig.

patterns.title: TS18046 — value is unknown
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` has type `unknown` (often a caught error under `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, or a JSON/`any`-tightened value). You must narrow it before use.
fixes: Narrow it: `if ({1} instanceof Error) { ... }`.
Type-guard primitives: `if (typeof {1} === 'string') { ... }`.
Cast deliberately when you're sure: `({1} as MyType)`.
For a caught error: `const msg = {1} instanceof Error ? {1}.message : String({1});`.

patterns.title: command not found
patterns.diagnosis: The shell couldn't find an executable named `{1}` in any directory listed in your `$PATH`. Either it's misspelled, not installed, or its directory isn't on `$PATH`.
fixes: Check spelling — `{1}` may be a typo of a real command.
Install it (e.g. `apt install {1}`, `brew install {1}`, or your package manager).
If it lives somewhere odd, run it by full path (`/opt/bin/{1}`) or add that dir: `export PATH="$PATH:/opt/bin"`.
If `{1}` is your own script, make sure it's executable (`chmod +x`) and call it as `./{1}`.

patterns.title: Permission denied running a file
patterns.diagnosis: The shell found `{1}` but the OS refused to execute it. Usually the file lacks the execute bit, or it sits on a filesystem mounted `noexec`.
fixes: Add the execute bit: `chmod +x {1}`.
If it's a script, run it through its interpreter instead: `bash {1}` or `python3 {1}`.
Check ownership and mode with `ls -l {1}` — you may need `sudo` or to own the file.
If it's on a `noexec` mount (some `/tmp`, USB drives), copy it somewhere executable first.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: No such file or directory
patterns.diagnosis: The path `{1}` doesn't exist from your current directory. For a script this also fires when the shebang line points at a missing interpreter.
fixes: Confirm the path with `ls -l {1}` and check you're in the right `pwd`.
Watch for relative vs absolute paths and a stray leading/trailing space.
If `{1}` is a script that exists, the shebang interpreter may be missing — check line 1 (`#!/bin/bash`) actually exists.
On scripts edited in Windows, a `\r` after the shebang path causes this — run `dos2unix {1}`.

patterns.title: Syntax error near unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: Bash hit `{1}` where it didn't expect it. Common causes: an unclosed quote/paren earlier in the line, a missing `;` or newline before a `do`/`then`, or copy-pasted smart quotes.
fixes: Look just BEFORE `{1}` for an unbalanced quote, `(`, `{`, or `[`.
If `{1}` is `(`, you may need `$(...)` for command substitution or `((...))` for arithmetic.
Add a separator: `if [ x = y ]; then` (the `;` before `then` is required).
Run `bash -n script.sh` to syntax-check without executing.

patterns.match: syntax error: unexpected end of file
patterns.title: Unexpected end of file
patterns.diagnosis: Bash reached the end of the script while still waiting for something to close — an unterminated `if`/`do`/`case`/function block, a missing `fi`/`done`/`esac`, or an unclosed quote or heredoc.
fixes: Match every opener to its closer: `if`→`fi`, `for`/`while`→`done`, `case`→`esac`, `{`→`}`.
Check for an unclosed `"` or `'` — everything after it gets swallowed.
If you use a heredoc, the closing delimiter must be at the start of a line with no trailing spaces.
Run `bash -n script.sh` to locate the unbalanced block.

patterns.title: Unbound variable (set -u)
patterns.diagnosis: You referenced `${1}` but it was never set, and `set -u` (nounset) is active so bash aborts instead of expanding to empty.
fixes: Set `{1}` before using it, or check spelling/case (bash vars are case-sensitive).
Provide a default: `"${{1}:-fallback}"` expands to `fallback` when unset.
For "is it set at all" use `"${{1}:-}"` to safely test, then branch.
If a variable is legitimately optional, guard it rather than disabling `set -u`.

patterns.title: Spaces around = in an assignment
patterns.diagnosis: Bash read `{1}` as a command because you put spaces around `=`. Variable assignment must have NO spaces: `{1}=value`, not `{1} = value`.
fixes: Remove the spaces: `{1}={2}` (no space before or after `=`).
To quote a value with spaces: `{1}="some value"`.
Inside `[ ... ]` the `=` IS spaced — don't confuse a test with an assignment.
For arithmetic use `(( {1} = 5 ))` where spaces are allowed.

patterns.title: Integer expression expected
patterns.diagnosis: A numeric `test` operator (`-eq`, `-lt`, `-gt`, etc.) got the non-numeric value `{1}`. Often the variable is empty or holds a string.
fixes: Use `-eq`/`-lt`/`-gt` only for integers; use `=`/`!=` to compare strings.
Quote and default the variable: `[ "${var:-0}" -eq 1 ]` so an empty value doesn't break it.
Strip non-digits first, or validate with a regex before the numeric test.
For arithmetic comparisons prefer `(( var > 1 ))` which is cleaner with numbers.

patterns.title: Unary operator expected
patterns.diagnosis: A `[ ... ]` test like `[ $var = x ]` expanded to too few words because `$var` was empty, leaving `[ = x ]`. Bash sees `=` with nothing on its left.
fixes: Quote the variable: `[ "$var" = x ]` so an empty value stays one (empty) argument.
Put the literal first to be safe: `[ x = "$var" ]`.
Use `[[ ... ]]` instead of `[ ... ]` — it tolerates empty unquoted vars.
Default the value: `[ "${var:-}" = x ]`.

patterns.title: [[ not found (wrong shell)
patterns.diagnosis: `[[ ]]` is a bash/ksh/zsh keyword, not POSIX `sh`. Your script ran under `sh` (or `dash`), where `[[` isn't a command, so it failed.
fixes: Use the bash shebang `#!/bin/bash` (or `#!/usr/bin/env bash`) and run with bash, not `sh script.sh`.
Or rewrite the test in POSIX form using single brackets: `[ "$a" = "$b" ]`.
Don't invoke a bash script with `sh file.sh` — that ignores the shebang.
Confirm your shell: `bash --version` vs `sh` being dash on Debian/Ubuntu.

patterns.match: bash: cannot create temp file for here-document: ([^\n]+)
patterns.title: Cannot create heredoc temp file
patterns.diagnosis: Bash writes heredoc contents to a temp file under `$TMPDIR`/`/tmp`, but couldn't ({1}). Usually the temp dir is full, missing, or not writable.
fixes: Check disk space with `df -h /tmp` — a full disk is the usual culprit.
Verify `/tmp` exists and is writable; set `TMPDIR` to a writable dir if not.
Clean out stale files if `/tmp` is out of inodes (`df -i`).
In sandboxes without `/tmp`, point `TMPDIR` at a real path: `export TMPDIR=$HOME/tmp`.

patterns.match: warning: here-document at line (\d+) delimited by end-of-file \(wanted `([^']+)'\)
patterns.title: Unterminated heredoc
patterns.diagnosis: A heredoc started at line {1} expected the closing word `{2}` on its own line, but the file ended first. The delimiter is missing, misspelled, or indented.
fixes: Put `{2}` alone on a line at column 1 (no leading spaces) to close the heredoc.
If you used `<<-{2}` you may indent ONLY with tabs, not spaces.
Check the closing word matches exactly, including case.
Don't add a trailing space after the closing `{2}`.

patterns.match: bash: cd: ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: cd: directory doesn't exist
patterns.diagnosis: `cd` couldn't find the directory `{1}`. It's the wrong path, a file (not a dir), or it expanded from an empty/unset variable.
fixes: Check the path exists and is a directory: `ls -ld {1}`.
If `{1}` came from a variable, it may be empty — quote and validate it first.
Watch for `~` not expanding inside quotes: `cd "$HOME/proj"` not `cd "~/proj"`.
In scripts, `cd dir || exit 1` so you don't keep running in the wrong place.

patterns.title: cd: target is a file, not a directory
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to `cd` into `{1}`, but `{1}` exists as a regular file (or a component of the path is a file), not a directory.
fixes: Run `ls -l {1}` — if it's a file, `cd` to its parent: `cd "$(dirname {1})"`.
Check each path component; a middle segment may be a file.
If you meant to operate on the file, use the file directly instead of `cd`.
Fix the variable or argument that produced the path.

patterns.title: Ambiguous redirect
patterns.diagnosis: A redirect target like `> {1}` expanded to zero or multiple words, so bash can't tell which file to use. Usually an unquoted variable that's empty or contains spaces.
fixes: Quote the target: `> "$file"` instead of `> $file`.
Check the variable isn't empty — an empty filename triggers this.
If the name legitimately has spaces or globs, quoting fixes it.
For `&>` style redirects, ensure you're using bash, not `sh`.

patterns.title: Redirect/open: permission denied
patterns.diagnosis: Bash couldn't open `/{1}` for the operation requested (often `>` redirecting output) because you lack write permission on the file or its directory. Note: `sudo cmd > /file` redirects as YOUR user, not root.
fixes: Check perms: `ls -l /{1}` and the parent dir's write bit.
`sudo` doesn't cover the redirect — use `cmd | sudo tee /{1}` instead of `sudo cmd > /{1}`.
Write somewhere you own (e.g. under `$HOME`) if root isn't required.
Fix ownership/mode with `sudo chown`/`chmod` if appropriate.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): No such file or directory\n.*input file is the same as output file
patterns.title: Redirect truncates the input file
patterns.diagnosis: A pipeline like `cmd file > file` truncated `{1}` to empty BEFORE the command read it, because the shell opens the `>` target first. The file is now blank.
fixes: Use a temp file: `cmd {1} > tmp && mv tmp {1}`.
Use a tool with in-place mode: `sed -i`, `awk -i inplace`, or `sponge` from moreutils.
Never read and write the same file in one redirect.
If data is lost, restore from backup/VCS.
patterns.example_fix: grep keep in.txt > out.tmp && mv out.tmp in.txt

patterns.match: bash: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
patterns.title: fork: resource temporarily unavailable
patterns.diagnosis: The system can't create new processes — you've hit a process/thread limit (`ulimit -u`), run out of PIDs, or a fork bomb / runaway loop is spawning endlessly.
fixes: Check limits: `ulimit -u` (max user processes) and raise it if appropriate.
Find the culprit: `ps -eLf | wc -l` and look for runaway processes to kill.
Look for an unbounded loop spawning subprocesses (missing wait/sleep, `&` in a tight loop).
Free memory/PIDs; a system near OOM also fails to fork.

patterns.title: Argument list too long
patterns.diagnosis: A glob or argument expansion (around `{1}`) produced more bytes than the kernel's `ARG_MAX` for a single command line — typically `rm *` in a directory with huge numbers of files.
fixes: Pipe through xargs: `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm`.
Use `find ... -delete` or `find ... -exec rm {} +` to batch arguments.
Process in chunks rather than globbing everything at once.
Check the real limit with `getconf ARG_MAX`.

patterns.title: Bad substitution
patterns.diagnosis: Bash couldn't parse the `${...}` expansion in `{1}`. Common causes: a typo in the parameter-expansion syntax, or using a bash-only form (`${var//a/b}`, `${var^^}`) under `sh`/dash.
fixes: Check the braces and operators: `${var:-default}`, `${var#prefix}`, `${#var}` (length).
If you used `${var//x/y}` or `${var^^}`, run under bash, not `sh`.
Command substitution is `$(...)` — a lone `${...}` for a command is wrong.
Run `bash -n` and re-read the parameter-expansion section of `man bash`.

patterns.title: ! triggers history expansion
patterns.diagnosis: In an interactive shell, `!{1}` was interpreted as a history-expansion reference (recall a past command), not literal text. Double-quoted strings still expand `!`.
fixes: Use single quotes for literal `!`: `echo 'Hello!'` instead of double quotes.
Escape it inside double quotes: `"Hello\!"`.
Disable history expansion in scripts/sessions: `set +H`.
This only bites interactively — scripts run non-interactively usually don't expand `!`.

patterns.title: Is a directory
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to read/execute/redirect `{1}` as if it were a file, but it's a directory. e.g. `cat dir`, `source dir`, or `> dir`.
fixes: Point at a file inside it: `cat {1}/somefile`.
To list contents use `ls {1}`; to find files use `find {1} -type f`.
If you meant to remove a directory, use `rm -r {1}` (or `rmdir` if empty).
Check the variable that produced `{1}` — it may be missing the filename portion.

patterns.title: printf: invalid number
patterns.diagnosis: A `%d`/`%i`/`%f` conversion in `printf` got the non-numeric value `{1}`. The argument has letters, spaces, or is empty.
fixes: Use `%s` if the value isn't actually a number.
Strip non-digits or validate the value before formatting.
Quote and default the variable: `printf '%d\n' "${n:-0}"`.
Leading/trailing whitespace counts — trim it first.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): No such file or directory\n.*: line (\d+):
patterns.title: Script can't find a referenced file
patterns.diagnosis: At line {2}, the script referenced `{1}` which doesn't exist relative to the current working directory. Scripts don't automatically run from their own folder.
fixes: Reference files relative to the script dir: `cd "$(dirname "$0")"` or use an absolute path.
Confirm `pwd` at runtime — `cd` earlier in the script may have moved you.
Quote the path in case it contains spaces.
Validate before use: `[ -f "{1}" ] || { echo missing; exit 1; }`.

patterns.match: bash: line (\d+): ([^:]+): No such file or directory
patterns.title: Bad interpreter / missing command at a line
patterns.diagnosis: On line {1}, bash tried to run `{2}` but couldn't find it. If `{2}` is the shebang interpreter, the path is wrong; otherwise it's a missing command on `$PATH`.
fixes: If `{2}` is a shebang path, fix it — prefer `#!/usr/bin/env bash` over a hard-coded path.
Check for a Windows `\r` line ending on the shebang: `dos2unix script.sh`.
Install or correct the command name `{2}`.
Verify `$PATH` includes where `{2}` lives.

patterns.title: noclobber prevents overwrite
patterns.diagnosis: `set -o noclobber` is on, so `>` refused to overwrite the existing file `{1}` (a safety feature to avoid clobbering data).
fixes: Force the overwrite intentionally with `>|`: `cmd >| {1}`.
Append instead of overwrite with `>>` if that's what you want.
Remove or rename `{1}` first if it's safe.
Disable the option for the session: `set +o noclobber`.

patterns.title: Cannot execute binary file
patterns.diagnosis: You tried to run `{1}` directly but it's a binary built for a different architecture/OS (or a data file, not an executable). The kernel can't load it.
fixes: Check the file type: `file {1}` — it'll show the target arch (e.g. ARM vs x86-64).
Get the right build for your platform, or run under emulation (qemu/Rosetta).
If it's a script missing a shebang, run it explicitly: `bash {1}`.
Make sure you didn't download an HTML error page instead of the binary.

patterns.title: exec format error
patterns.diagnosis: The kernel refused to exec the file because its format/architecture is unrecognized — wrong CPU arch, a corrupted binary, or a script whose shebang interpreter is itself the wrong format.
fixes: Run `file <prog>` to see what arch/format it actually is.
Install the version matching your CPU (arm64 vs amd64).
If it's a text script, add a valid shebang line as line 1.
Re-download — a truncated/corrupt binary triggers this too.

patterns.title: kill: no such process
patterns.diagnosis: You signaled PID {1} but no process with that ID exists — it already exited, or the PID was wrong/stale (e.g. read from an out-of-date pidfile).
fixes: Confirm the PID is alive: `ps -p {1}` or `kill -0 {1}`.
It likely already exited — that's often fine; guard with `kill -0 {1} 2>/dev/null`.
If reading from a pidfile, the file may be stale; clean it up.
To kill by name instead: `pkill -f name` or `kill $(pgrep name)`.

patterns.match: bash: wait: pid (\d+) is not a child of this shell
patterns.title: wait: not a child of this shell
patterns.diagnosis: `wait {1}` only works on background jobs THIS shell started. PID {1} was started by a different shell/subshell or isn't a tracked child, so wait can't reap it.
fixes: Capture the PID right after backgrounding: `cmd & pid=$!; wait "$pid"`.
Don't `wait` on PIDs spawned inside a subshell `( ... )` or another process.
If you need to wait for an unrelated process, poll `kill -0 PID` in a loop instead.
`wait` with no args waits for all of this shell's background jobs.

patterns.match: bash: ([^:]+): syntax error: operand expected \(error token is "([^"]*)"\)
patterns.title: Arithmetic: operand expected
patterns.diagnosis: An arithmetic context `(( ))`/`$(( ))` in `{1}` expected a number but got `{2}` (or empty). Often an unset variable, a non-numeric value, or a stray operator.
fixes: Default the variable: `(( ${n:-0} + 1 ))` so empty becomes 0.
Ensure the value is purely numeric — strip letters/spaces first.
Don't put a `$` on a bare leading operator; check for a missing operand around `{2}`.
Inside `(( ))` you don't need `$` on variable names: `(( i + 1 ))`.

patterns.title: Arithmetic division by zero
patterns.diagnosis: An arithmetic expression in `{1}` divided (or took modulo) by zero — usually because a divisor variable was empty/unset and expanded to 0.
fixes: Guard the divisor: `(( d != 0 )) && (( r = n / d ))`.
Default unset variables so they don't silently become 0 in a divisor.
Validate inputs before the calculation.
For floating-point division, bash can't do it natively — use `bc` or `awk`.

patterns.title: Cannot assign to readonly variable
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` was marked `readonly` (or `declare -r`) earlier, so this assignment is rejected. Readonly is permanent for the shell's lifetime.
fixes: Use a different variable name if you need a mutable value.
Don't re-declare it; remove the earlier `readonly {1}` if it shouldn't be constant.
A readonly cannot be unset or reassigned — start a new shell to clear it.
Check you aren't shadowing a special readonly like `UID`, `PPID`, or `BASHPID`.

patterns.title: Not a valid identifier
patterns.diagnosis: A command like `export`, `declare`, `read`, or `local` got `{1}`, which isn't a legal variable name. Names must start with a letter/underscore and contain only letters, digits, and underscores.
fixes: Remove illegal characters (hyphens, dots, spaces) — `my-var` is invalid, use `my_var`.
Don't put `$` on the name when declaring: `export FOO=1`, not `export $FOO=1`.
With `read`, pass the variable NAME not its value: `read foo`, not `read $foo`.
Names can't start with a digit.

patterns.title: Too many open files
patterns.diagnosis: The process hit its file-descriptor limit while handling `{1}`. Usually a loop opens files/sockets without closing them, leaking descriptors until `ulimit -n` is reached.
fixes: Raise the limit if legitimate: `ulimit -n 4096` (and configure it persistently).
Close descriptors you open — don't leave files/pipes/sockets dangling in a loop.
Inspect open FDs: `ls -l /proc/$$/fd` or `lsof -p <pid>`.
Reuse a single connection/handle instead of opening one per iteration.

patterns.title: Declared and not used
patterns.diagnosis: Go treats an unused local variable `{1}` as a compile error — every declared local must be read at least once.
fixes: Remove the declaration of `{1}` if you don't need it.
Actually use `{1}` somewhere, even just by logging it.
Assign it to the blank identifier to discard it: `_ = {1}`.
patterns.example_fix:
x := compute()
_ = x // or just delete the line if x is never needed

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?(?:imported and not used|"([^"]+)" imported and not used)
patterns.title: Imported and not used
patterns.diagnosis: You imported the package "{1}" but never referenced anything from it. Go rejects unused imports.
fixes: Delete the import line for "{1}" if it isn't needed.
If you only want its init() side effects, blank-import it: `import _ "{1}"`.
Run `goimports -w .` or rely on `gofmt`/your editor to auto-remove unused imports.

patterns.title: Undefined identifier
patterns.diagnosis: The compiler can't find a declaration for `{1}` in scope. It's misspelled, unexported, not imported, or simply not declared.
fixes: Check spelling and case — `{1}` must match exactly, and exported names start with a capital letter.
If `{1}` lives in another package, import that package and qualify it (`pkg.{1}`).
Make sure the file defining `{1}` is in the same package and part of the build.

patterns.title: Type mismatch in assignment/argument
patterns.diagnosis: You passed `{1}`, which is a `{2}`, where a `{3}` was required. Go has no implicit numeric or interface conversions.
fixes: Convert explicitly if the types are compatible: `{3}({1})`.
Check the function signature — you may be passing the wrong argument.
If `{3}` is an interface, ensure `{2}` actually implements all of its methods.
patterns.example_fix: var f float64 = float64(myInt) // explicit conversion

patterns.title: Missing return at end of function
patterns.diagnosis: A function declared with a return type has a code path that reaches the end without returning a value.
fixes: Add a final `return` covering the fall-through path.
If a switch/if covers all cases, the compiler still needs a terminating statement — add a `return` or `panic("unreachable")` after it.
Use a `default` case that returns, so every branch yields a value.

patterns.match: panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
patterns.title: Nil pointer dereference
patterns.diagnosis: Your code dereferenced a pointer (or called a method on a nil interface/pointer) that was nil. The goroutine panicked at runtime.
fixes: Guard with `if p != nil` before dereferencing.
Make sure constructors actually allocate: use `&T{}` or `new(T)` before use.
A nil map can be read but not written — initialize with `make(map[K]V)` before assigning.
Read the SIGSEGV stack trace below the panic line to find the exact dereference.

patterns.match: panic: runtime error: index out of range \[(\d+)\] with length (\d+)
patterns.title: Slice/array index out of range
patterns.diagnosis: You indexed element {1} of a slice/array whose length is {2}, so the highest valid index is {3}. Indices are 0-based.
fixes: Loop with `for i := range s` or `for i := 0; i < len(s); i++` so i never reaches len(s).
Check the length with `len(s)` before indexing.
Off-by-one: the last valid index is len-1, not len.

patterns.match: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range \[:(\d+)\] with capacity (\d+)
patterns.title: Slice bounds out of range
patterns.diagnosis: A slice expression asked for index {1}, but the slice's capacity is only {2}. Reslicing can't exceed the underlying array's capacity.
fixes: Clamp the high bound: `s[:min(n, len(s))]`.
Check `len(s)` (or `cap(s)`) before slicing.
Use `append` to grow a slice instead of reslicing past its capacity.

patterns.match: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
patterns.title: Deadlock — all goroutines blocked
patterns.diagnosis: Every goroutine (including main) is blocked forever, usually on a channel send/receive that no one will satisfy, or on a Mutex/WaitGroup that's never released.
fixes: An unbuffered channel needs a concurrent receiver before a send unblocks — start the receiving goroutine first, or use a buffered channel.
Make sure something actually closes the channel or sends the value you're waiting on.
Check WaitGroup counts: `Add` before launching, `Done` exactly once per goroutine, `Wait` after.
Don't `Lock` a Mutex twice in the same goroutine without unlocking.

patterns.match: panic: (?:send on closed channel|close of closed channel|close of nil channel)
patterns.title: Channel misuse panic
patterns.diagnosis: You sent on a closed channel, closed a channel twice, or closed a nil channel. Only one owner should close, and only once.
fixes: Make the sender the only party that closes the channel, and close it exactly once.
Never send after `close(ch)` — receivers should detect closure via `v, ok := <-ch`.
Initialize the channel with `make(chan T)` before closing; closing nil panics.
Use `sync.Once` or a done-channel pattern to guard the close.

patterns.match: panic: assignment to entry in nil map
patterns.title: Assignment to nil map
patterns.diagnosis: You wrote to a map that was declared but never allocated. A nil map can be read but not written.
fixes: Allocate before writing: `m := make(map[K]V)`.
For a struct field, initialize it in your constructor or with a composite literal `{M: map[K]V{}}`.
Reading a nil map is fine and returns the zero value — only assignment panics.

patterns.title: Failed type assertion
patterns.diagnosis: A type assertion expected `{3}` but the interface `{1}` actually held a `{2}`, so the single-value assertion panicked.
fixes: Use the two-value form so a bad assertion doesn't panic: `v, ok := x.({3}); if !ok { ... }`.
Assert to the type the value really is (`{2}`), or handle both with a type switch.
Print the dynamic type with `fmt.Printf("%T\n", x)` to confirm what's actually inside.

patterns.match: panic: runtime error: integer divide by zero
patterns.title: Integer divide by zero
patterns.diagnosis: An integer division or modulo had a zero divisor, which panics at runtime (unlike floats, which yield Inf/NaN).
fixes: Guard the divisor: `if d != 0 { q = n / d }`.
Validate user/computed input before dividing.
If a float result is acceptable, convert first: `float64(n) / float64(d)` gives Inf instead of panicking.

patterns.title: Syntax error — unexpected token
patterns.diagnosis: The parser hit `{1}` where it didn't belong{2}. Often a stray/missing brace, a misplaced statement, or a newline auto-inserting a semicolon.
fixes: Check brace/paren balance around the reported line.
Go's opening `{` must be on the same line as `if`/`for`/`func` — a `{` on its own line breaks things.
Run `gofmt -e file.go` to pinpoint the exact location.
Look for a missing comma in a composite literal or argument list.

patterns.title: Statement at package level
patterns.diagnosis: You put an executable statement (assignment, call, etc.) directly at file scope. Only declarations (var/const/type/func/import) are allowed there.
fixes: Move the statement inside a function (e.g. `func main()` or `func init()`).
At package scope use `var x = ...` declarations, not `x := ...` or bare expressions.
If it's setup code, put it in `func init()` which runs automatically.
patterns.example_fix: var greeting = "hi" // declaration is OK at package level

patterns.title: Expected declaration at top level
patterns.diagnosis: At file scope Go expects a declaration keyword (package/import/var/const/type/func), but found `{1}`.
fixes: Make sure the file starts with a `package` clause.
Wrap top-level code in a function — only declarations live at file scope.
Check for a missing closing `}` on the function above, which spills code into package scope.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?([\w.]+) redeclared (?:in this block|as imported package name)
patterns.title: Redeclared identifier
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is declared more than once in the same scope (or clashes with an imported package name). Go forbids duplicate declarations in one block.
fixes: Rename one of the two `{1}` declarations.
If you meant to reassign, use `=` instead of `:=`.
Avoid naming a variable the same as an imported package.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?no new variables on left side of :=
patterns.title: No new variables with :=
patterns.diagnosis: Short declaration `:=` requires at least one brand-new variable on the left. Every name here already exists in this scope.
fixes: Use plain assignment `=` since all variables already exist.
Introduce at least one new name on the left to keep `:=`.
Watch for accidental shadowing where you thought a name was new.
patterns.example_fix: x = compute() // not x := compute() if x already declared

patterns.title: Type doesn't satisfy interface
patterns.diagnosis: `{1}` is being used as a `{2}`, but it lacks the `{3}` method, so it doesn't implement the interface.
fixes: Add the missing method `{3}` to `{1}` with the exact signature the interface requires.
Check the receiver: a method on `*{1}` only satisfies the interface for a `*{1}` value, not a `{1}`.
Match the method signature exactly — parameter and return types must align, names need not.

patterns.match: (?:\.go:\d+:\d+: )?(?:not enough|too many) (?:arguments|return values) (?:in call to|to return)
patterns.title: Wrong number of arguments/returns
patterns.diagnosis: The call or `return` doesn't match the function signature's arity. Go requires exact argument and return counts.
fixes: Re-check the function's declared parameters and return values.
For variadic functions pass a slice with `...`: `f(args...)`.
When returning multiple values, list all of them (use `_` to discard ones you don't need).
